introduction: A good security briefing gives the team enough information to work safely and consistently without burying them in unnecessary detail. The aim is simple: make sure every officer starts the shift clear on risks, priorities, incidents, equipment, patrol expectations and escalation points.
keyTakeaways: Start the briefing with the live risk picture, not generic reminders.
Separate patrol priorities, incident follow-ups and equipment issues.
Use plain English so instructions can be followed under pressure.
Record escalation points and supervisor decisions clearly.
Use AI prompts only to structure drafts, never to replace supervisor judgement.

content:
## Direct answer

A security briefing template should cover the current risk picture, priority patrols, known incidents, expected visitors or contractors, equipment issues, escalation rules, welfare points and the exact handover actions needed before the next shift. Keep it short enough to use every day and specific enough to guide real decisions.

## The shift briefing template

Use this structure before each shift:

- **Current risk picture:** what changed since the last shift and what the team must watch closely.
- **Priority patrols:** locations, times, access points and any patrol instructions that differ from normal.
- **Open incidents:** incident references, current status, evidence still needed and manager follow-up.
- **People and movements:** expected visitors, contractors, deliveries, VIPs or known exclusions.
- **Equipment and systems:** radios, keys, body-worn cameras, alarms, access control and CCTV issues.
- **Escalation rules:** who to call, when to call them and what must be recorded.
- **Handover actions:** what the outgoing team must complete before leaving post.

## Why plain English matters

Security briefings are used when people are tired, distracted or under pressure. Plain English reduces the chance of missed instructions. The UK government's plain English guidance says public information should be clear and easy to understand: [GOV.UK content design guidance](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/content-design/writing-for-gov-uk).

That principle applies to security operations too. A briefing that says "check the rear delivery gate at 21:00 and 23:00 because the latch failed yesterday" is more useful than "remain vigilant around vulnerable access points".

## How AI can help without taking control

AI can help a supervisor turn rough notes into a cleaner briefing, but it should not decide the risk picture. Use AI to structure, simplify and check clarity. Keep responsibility with the supervisor.

A useful prompt is:

**Turn these shift notes into a clear security briefing. Keep the facts, split actions by patrols, incidents, equipment and escalation, and flag anything that needs supervisor confirmation before it is briefed to officers.**

## Practical example

Rough note:

"Gate 3 still sticking, contractor due around 10, report from last night about youths near east fence, radio 4 poor battery, new guard on B patrol."

Briefing version:

- Gate 3 is still sticking. Check it during each external patrol and report if it fails to close.
- Contractor expected around 10:00. Confirm ID and sign-in before access.
- East fence needs extra attention after last night's report of youths nearby.
- Radio 4 has battery issues. Do not issue it until charged and checked.
- New officer assigned to B patrol must be shown the patrol route before first round.

## Supervisor checks before briefing

Before you brief the team, check:

- Are the instructions accurate and current?
- Is anything sensitive removed or limited to those who need to know?
- Does each action have an owner?
- Are escalation points clear?
- Is the language simple enough to follow quickly?

The Health and Safety Executive provides practical guidance for keeping workplace health and safety simple and understandable: [HSE simple health and safety](https://www.hse.gov.uk/simple-health-safety/). Security briefings should follow the same practical standard.

## Related security workflows

If your briefing reveals poor handover quality, use the guide on [writing better security handover notes](/blog/how-to-write-better-security-handover-notes). If the issue is incident quality, read [how to write a clear security incident report](/blog/how-to-write-a-clear-security-incident-report-that-managers-can-act-on). For recurring tasks, strengthen the underlying process with [AI-assisted security SOPs](/blog/how-to-create-a-security-sop-with-ai-without-losing-operational-control).

## Call to action

Use 100 Security Prompts to turn messy operational notes into clearer briefings, handovers and SOP drafts. Keep supervisor review in place, keep the instructions practical, and use AI as a structure tool rather than an operational decision-maker.
